bib.title: An Empirical Study of GPT-3 for Few-Shot Knowledge-Based VQA

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Yang, Gan, Wang, Hu, Lu, Liu, Wang (Microsoft), "An Empirical Study of GPT-3 for Few-Shot Knowledge-Based VQA" (PICa), AAAI 2022. The extraction is arXiv:2109.05014v2.

COVERAGE: All 10 pages, about 62,194 of 62,194 characters, including the references and the supplementary Figure 5 text. pypdf printed one harmless FloatObject warning. Figure-internal text (the qualitative panels) comes out jumbled but can still be read. I skimmed the references.

CLAIMS
- claim: With a text-only GPT-3 fed captions plus tags, PICa beats the best fully supervised method on OK-VQA by 8.6 points with no fine-tuning.
  number: 48.0 vs 39.4 (MAVEx), 16 shots
  setup: OK-VQA test set (14,055 image-question pairs, VQAv2 soft accuracy). GPT-3 175B, frozen. Captions from VinVL-base fine-tuned on COCO-train14, tags from the Azure tagging API, PICa-Full.
  quote: "PICa-Full achieves an accuracy of 48.0% with 16 in-context VQA examples, compared with the supervised state-of-the-art accuracy of 39.4% trained on the entire OK-VQA training set."
  where: p.4, Table 1
- claim: More shots help. n=16 is about the most that fits in GPT-3's 2049-token input.
  number: 40.8 at n=1 to 48.0 at n=16. Zero-shot is 17.1.
  setup: PICa-Full with captions plus tags (Table 2, row e). Frozen at 7B scores 12.6 at n=4.
  quote: "more shots generally lead to better performance, e.g., 40.8% when n = 1 to 48.0% when n = 16"; "n = 16 is roughly the max number of examples that GPT-3 can take, with a max input length of 2049."
  where: p.4–5, Table 2
- claim: Picking in-context examples by similarity beats random picks. Dissimilar examples do worse than random.
  number: random 43.3, question-similar 45.8, image only 44.1, question+image 46.5, dissimilar 40.1. The oracle that also matches on the answer reaches 49.1.
  setup: OK-VQA, 16 shots, CLIP ViT-B/16 cosine similarity (RoBERTa scores 45.4 for question-similar). Table 4.
  quote: "PICa-Full jointly considers the question and image similarities, and further improves the accuracy to 46.5%"
  where: p.5–6, Table 4
- claim: Multi-query ensembling gives a further gain. It sends k prompts, each with different selected examples, and keeps the answer with the highest summed log-probability.
  number: 46.5 (k=1) to 47.7 (k=3) to 48.0 (k=5) at n=16. At n=1 the jump is 36.4 to 40.8.
  setup: OK-VQA, with question+image example selection in place. Table 5.
  quote: "(b) k=1 36.4 43.0 46.5 (c) k=3 40.0 45.2 47.7 (d) k=5 40.8 45.4 48.0"
  where: p.6, Table 5
- claim: Accuracy depends on how much the text says about the image. Captions plus tags beat either one alone, and oracle human captions show how far a better description could go.
  number: blind 30.1; tags 44.6; COCO caption 46.9; caption+tags 48.0; 1 GT caption 48.7; all 5 GT captions 53.3. A captioner trained only on Conceptual Captions (no COCO) still gets 44.0.
  setup: OK-VQA, PICa-Full, 16 shots. Table 3.
  quote: "Concatenating all the ground-truth captions as shown in row (g) provides a more thorough description of the image content, thus further improving the accuracy to 53.3%"; "we find that detailed and thorough descriptions lead to better VQA performance."
  where: p.5, Table 3
- claim: Turning the image into text first costs accuracy on questions about visual detail. On VQAv2, PICa trails supervised models by about 17 points.
  number: 56.1 vs Oscar 73.8. Frozen scores 38.2. With 5 GT captions PICa reaches 59.7.
  setup: VQAv2 validation set, answers generated open-ended. Table 6.
  quote: "Compared with the supervised performance of 73.8% by Oscar (Li et al. 2020), the proposed method is still around 17% lower in accuracy"
  where: p.7, Table 6

LIMITS
- The authors concede this point directly: "one limitation of our method is that the image is abstracted as text. Captions or tags only provide a partial description of the image, and might miss important visual details" (p.7). The failures they show are colour (the jacket is red, PICa says "black") and counting ("3" giraffes when the truth is 6–8). The successes on colour are often guesses: "bedroom walls are usually white." They expect that "an end-to-end vision encoder tuning can help answer such questions better."
- The VQAv2 human baselines they cite measure the same text bottleneck in people: "40.8% with questions only, and 57.5% with questions and captions, compared with 83.3% with both questions and images" (p.7).
- The text-only GPT-3 still scores 30.1 with no image at all (blind), so part of the OK-VQA result comes from language priors.
- Only COCO photos are tested, with no charts, documents or diagrams. The source does not show whether the caption route works for charts.
- Their best captioner is fine-tuned on COCO, the same image distribution as the test set. The variant that never saw COCO falls to 44.0.
- Open-ended answers make scoring hard; the authors note this themselves. The rationales are generated zero-shot and are not validated.
- Dated: GPT-3 davinci (175B) with a 2049-token limit, and the API only. They say "inaccessibility of the GPT-3 raw model makes it difficult to conduct an in-depth analysis." There is no compute or cost reporting.

BUILDS ON: GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020, arXiv); LMs as knowledge bases (Petroni et al. 2019, arXiv); Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al. 2021, arXiv); in-context example selection (Liu et al. 2021, arXiv "What Makes Good In-Context Examples for GPT-3?"); log-probability answer ranking (Chen et al. 2021, Codex, arXiv); VinVL (Zhang et al. 2021, CVPR); CLIP (Radford et al. 2021, arXiv); OK-VQA (Marino et al. 2019, CVPR); VQAv2 (Goyal et al. 2017, CVPR). Baselines are KRISP (Marino et al. 2021, CVPR) and MAVEx (Wu et al. 2021, arXiv). Code: https://github.com/microsoft/PICa.

CODE: none. The prompt format is in Figure 2 (p.3): the head "Please answer the question according to the above context.", then n blocks of the form "Context: <caption> === Q: <q> A: <a> ===", then the test block.

FIGURES
- Figure 2, p.3: "Inference-time interface of PICa for n-shot VQA. The input prompt to GPT-3 consists of a prompt head h (blue box), n in-context examples ... and the VQA input x (green box)." It shows the whole pipeline (caption, then text prompt, then frozen LLM) in one image. It fits "Separate seeing from reasoning."
- Alternative, Figure 4, p.7: VQAv2 successes and failures (the colour and giraffe-count errors). It makes the "what is lost" point concretely.

PROBLEMS: The figure panels extract out of order and some are duplicated. The tables extracted cleanly. I found no embedded instructions. I ran the figure-captions script only by reading captions in the text, not with figures.py. The full extraction was written to /tmp/pica.txt.
